title: Dzvin.co Product Documentation
lead: Product positioning, customer value, capability map, demos and a ready-to-use presentation narrative.

articles.title: The Dzvin.co product story
articles.summary: What the product solves, what to sell and why it is more than a daily wellbeing tracker.

sections.title: One-sentence positioning
paragraphs: Dzvin.co combines personal observations, team-level insights and research workflows to turn wellbeing changes into understandable signals and practical next steps.

sections.title: 30-second pitch
paragraphs: Wellbeing information is often fragmented across check-ins, journals and separate reports. Individuals struggle to see a trajectory, managers recognize issues late and researchers find it hard to connect measurement with outcomes. Dzvin.co brings these jobs into one environment: individuals record their experience, organizations review permitted group-level patterns, and research teams structure programs and examine outcomes.

sections.title: The customer problem
paragraphs: A one-time check-in is a snapshot, not a trajectory. Even repeated measurements have limited value unless people can review changes, choose a next step and see what happens afterwards.
The core product narrative is 'observe → understand a trend → prioritize → act → check again'. It describes a workflow, not a promise that every intervention will work.

sections.title: Three product experiences
paragraphs: Personal: daily observations, history, exercises, goals and questionnaires. Organizational: roles, groups, team analytics, risk-event workflows and manager actions. Research: projects, cohorts, inspection, reporting artifacts and controlled access.
Each experience has a different user, buying rationale and output. A good presentation does not blur all three into one generic pitch.

sections.title: The strongest differentiator to explain
paragraphs: Do not open with 'we have AI and charts'. Open with the decision the audience makes without context today: what support should I try, which team needs attention or how do we evaluate a program?
Show the path from signal to managed action. Internal algorithms, model parameters and proprietary implementation are not needed to communicate the value.

sections.title: A tangible output for each user
paragraphs: Individuals get a timeline of observations and accessible next steps. Managers get an overview of team dynamics and signals to review. Researchers get a structured path from program design to observation and reporting.

sections.title: Public claims that can be supported
paragraphs: Describe user-visible modules, the types of observations captured, permitted roles, the ways data is grouped and the workflow from signal to action.
Avoid claiming proven reductions in burnout, guaranteed improvements in employee retention, model accuracy or financial ROI without independently verified evidence.

sections.title: Ready-to-use slide copy
paragraphs: Headline: 'From wellbeing signals to decisions you can examine.' Subtitle: 'One platform for individuals, organizations and research programs.'
Three supporting points: 'Capture consistent observations', 'Surface patterns and priorities', 'Organize follow-up actions and assess change'.

articles.title: Who Dzvin.co serves and why
articles.summary: Buyer concerns, user jobs, examples and presentation angles by segment.

sections.title: Individuals: the job to be done
paragraphs: People need a simple way to notice changes, stop relying on memory and move from a daily check-in to an accessible practice.
Show a check-in, the observation history, suggested exercises, goals and the next check-in. The takeaway is a coherent personal workflow.

sections.title: Individuals: scenario
paragraphs: After a demanding week, a user records stress, energy, focus and mood; reviews earlier entries; selects an available exercise; and checks in again the following day.
This is an illustrative scenario, not a testimonial or proof that the exercise caused an improvement.

sections.title: Companies: decision makers and users
paragraphs: Typical stakeholders include HR, People Operations, team leads and company leadership. Managers work with defined permissions, while administrators maintain the organizational structure and access.
The buyer asks 'Where is risk building up and how do we respond in time?' The manager asks 'Which permitted group or signal needs review today?'

sections.title: Companies: scenario
paragraphs: After a series of check-ins, a manager views aggregated analytics, changes the period and group selection, reviews risk events, opens details and records an appropriate follow-up action.
The value shown is a managed prioritization workflow, not automated employee evaluation.

sections.title: Research: decision makers and users
paragraphs: The research audience includes universities, research institutions, program leads and funding partners. Day-to-day users are authorized researchers and project administrators.
The buyer asks 'Can we standardize repeated observations, compare cohorts, control access and prepare program evidence?'

sections.title: Research: scenario
paragraphs: A research team creates a project, defines membership and cohorts, examines history and available inspection tools, requests an export and reviews the audit trail.
The output is a traceable research workflow, not a claim of validated intervention effects.

sections.title: Connecting the segments
paragraphs: Individual interactions create repeated observations. The team experience reviews permitted aggregated views. Research programs structure cohorts and track study-related outputs.
Present this as a related product family, while keeping scope, budgets, access and success criteria distinct.

sections.title: Questions before a presentation
paragraphs: Identify the buyer, the decision they need to make, the source of data, the expected output, access restrictions and the demo scenario. A team leader does not need a research export tour.
End with 'Which decision would your team like to make faster or with more context?' rather than a long feature checklist.

articles.title: Product capability map
articles.summary: Real user-facing modules, outputs, roles and what to show on screen.

sections.title: Personal check-ins
paragraphs: The standard check-in captures stress, mood, energy and focus. Personal areas also support journals or notes, exercises, short questionnaires, goals and progress review.
Slide message: 'Connected observations instead of isolated questionnaires.' Demo: record an entry, review history, choose a next step.

sections.title: Personal progress
paragraphs: History and statistics views help users review changes over time. Goals and short exercises connect measurement with possible next actions.
Slide message: 'See the progression, not just today's score.'

sections.title: Organization structure
paragraphs: Administrative screens provide groups and subgroups, membership, invites, roles and manager access to specified groups.
Slide message: 'Insights aligned with actual teams and permissions.' Avoid making an unsupported claim of guaranteed anonymity.

sections.title: Team analytics
paragraphs: Organization views include summary metrics, trends, risk distribution and group breakdowns. Authorized managers can change the time window and group selection.
Slide message: 'See where the situation is changing.' Demo: overview, period selection, group breakdown.

sections.title: Decision-support workflow
paragraphs: A dedicated management view combines summary reporting with a feed of risk events. The interface supports opening event details, follow-up actions and resolving events.
Slide message: 'A signal becomes a manageable workflow.' The product does not independently make personnel decisions.

sections.title: Research projects
paragraphs: The Research Workspace provides project lists, creation, participants, cohort settings, grant-related material and historical datasets.
Slide message: 'A managed program workspace from setup to analysis.' Access depends on authorized roles and program configuration.

sections.title: Research inspection and reporting
paragraphs: Research views include model-inspection surfaces, export requests and audit history. These support tracking work and building structured reporting materials.
Slide message: 'From collection to inspectable results.' Demonstrate only authorized, non-sensitive data.

sections.title: Permissions and availability
paragraphs: The app has distinct experiences for individuals, managers, administrators and researchers. A feature's inclusion in the capability map does not imply availability to every account.
The PO should record access prerequisites and the test environment needed for each demo.

sections.title: Verification maturity
paragraphs: A visible screen or an implemented API contract does not prove that a customer integration, complete end-to-end flow or a prediction's quality is independently validated.
Separate the labels 'visible in the product', 'verified through an end-to-end flow' and 'outcome measured with evidence'.

articles.title: End-to-end demonstration scripts
articles.summary: Screen sequence, presenter narrative and expected audience takeaway.

sections.title: Demo 1 — personal, 3–5 minutes
paragraphs: Start with: 'How do I see how I felt over several days?' Show a short check-in, the four dimensions, history, an available exercise and the next daily entry.
Final screen: the observation timeline. Presenter line: 'Your entries accumulate into a personal trajectory instead of disappearing into separate forms.'

sections.title: Demo 2 — organization, 5–7 minutes
paragraphs: Begin with an HR question: 'Which teams need our attention this week?' Show company groups and manager scope, then the analytics overview, trends and period filters.
Open the risk-event feed and a sample event. Explain how a manager moves from a signal to reviewing context and a follow-up action. Use only authorized demo data.

sections.title: Demo 3 — research, 5–7 minutes
paragraphs: Ask: 'How can we manage repeated observations in a structured program?' Show projects, the selected project overview, membership, cohort settings and historical data.
Finish with inspection, export-request and audit screens. The story is controlled research operations and traceability.

sections.title: Before presenting
paragraphs: Confirm the test account's role, prepare a sample project and group with non-personal records, ensure each screen has meaningful data and approve any screenshots.
If an environment cannot demonstrate a feature, mark it as not currently verified instead of staging fake live results.

sections.title: Turn demos into slides
paragraphs: For each step use three pieces: 'Customer situation → product screen → decision or observation enabled'. Highlight one part of the screenshot rather than showing an unreadable full dashboard.
Close each demo with a concrete artifact: an individual's history, a reviewed team priority or a structured research output.

sections.title: Questions to prepare for
paragraphs: 'Where does information come from?' — Voluntary entries, questionnaires and data relevant to the selected workflow. 'Who can view it?' — Authorized roles and configured permissions.
'How do you know an intervention works?' — Only make claims supported by a defined measurement and a verified outcome.

articles.title: Ready-to-use Dzvin.co presentation
articles.summary: Ten-slide deck narrative, copy blocks, short pitches and buyer questions.

sections.title: Slide 1 — proposition
paragraphs: Headline: 'Dzvin.co: from observation to action.' Subtitle: 'Personal wellbeing support, team analytics and research workflows in one platform.'
Visual: three connected product experiences — Individual, Organization, Research.

sections.title: Slide 2 — problem
paragraphs: Headline: 'Signals are everywhere. A useful picture is not.' Points: measurements are fragmented, changes are hard to compare, response is delayed and program outcomes are hard to assess.
Visual: separate inputs that do not lead to a next decision.

sections.title: Slide 3 — approach
paragraphs: Headline: 'One loop: observe → understand → prioritize → act → review.' Explain how the product organizes signals and next steps for different user roles.
Visual: a simple five-step product journey, not an internal algorithm diagram.

sections.title: Slide 4 — personal experience
paragraphs: Headline: 'A personal trajectory, not a one-off questionnaire.' Show daily check-ins, history, practices, goals and questionnaires.
Caption: 'A user records their state and returns to a clear next step.'

sections.title: Slide 5 — organizational experience
paragraphs: Headline: 'Team signals managers can work with.' Show groups, trends, risk distribution, events and the action workflow.
Caption: 'Group context → priority → managed follow-up.'

sections.title: Slide 6 — research experience
paragraphs: Headline: 'From an observation program to inspectable results.' Show projects, cohorts, history, inspection, export and audit.
Caption: 'A structured research workflow and materials for reporting.'

sections.title: Slide 7 — product distinction
paragraphs: Headline: 'More than a collection of tests and charts.' Three ideas: connected experiences, understanding change over time and checking what happened after action.
Avoid unsupported superlatives and comparisons with competitors.

sections.title: Slide 8 — first deployment
paragraphs: Headline: 'Start with one decision worth improving.' Steps: select the group, define observations, configure access, run a pilot, review usage and outcome measures.
Show a verification plan, not fabricated customer logos.

sections.title: Slide 9 — measures
paragraphs: Headline: 'Value deserves measurement.' Examples: participation continuity, data completeness, time from signal to review, changes in aggregate indicators and research-protocol completion.
Separate observed product usage from business impact that needs pilot confirmation.

sections.title: Slide 10 — next step
paragraphs: Headline: 'Test Dzvin.co in your own workflow.' Invite the audience to a focused demo or a pilot with an agreed audience, access model and criteria for success.
End with one question: 'Which decision is hardest today without a consistent picture?'

sections.title: Short pitch variants
paragraphs: For HR: 'Dzvin.co helps organizations understand changing team conditions and organize responses to risk signals.' For individuals: 'Dzvin.co turns short daily observations into a personal timeline and practical next steps.' For researchers: 'Dzvin.co structures cohorts, observations and evaluation workflows.'
Pair each pitch with the appropriate real screen, not a generic AI claim.

sections.title: Likely questions and answers
paragraphs: Why not just a survey? — Because observations connect to history, trends and follow-up workflows. What does a manager see? — Role-permitted group views, reports and risk events. How do we prove the value? — Agree on the outcome, observation window and evaluation method.
Which audience goes on the slide? — The audience that buys or uses the selected experience.

articles.title: PO product handbook
articles.summary: Align value, feature scope, proof, demos and measurable acceptance criteria.

sections.title: Separate problem, capability and outcome
paragraphs: Problem: the team leader cannot see changing patterns. Capability: a role-scoped team view with time filters. Product outcome: the manager knows which group to examine and which action to discuss.
A capability does not automatically establish a measured business effect. Keep these statements distinct in specs and sales materials.

sections.title: Role map
paragraphs: Individuals use check-ins, history, exercises and goals. Managers access permitted groups, analytics and risk events. Administrators set up organizational structure, membership and permissions. Researchers work with projects, cohorts, inspection and reporting.
Each user story should identify the role, permitted data, action and expected on-screen result.

sections.title: Acceptance: personal journey
paragraphs: Scenario: a user records a check-in, finds it in their history and returns to an available practice or goal.
Check persistence, timestamps, data isolation, empty states and error communication.

sections.title: Acceptance: organization journey
paragraphs: Scenario: a manager opens permitted groups, selects a period, reviews a trend and event, and records an allowed action.
Check authorization boundaries, missing data, event state transitions and handling of empty groups.

sections.title: Acceptance: research journey
paragraphs: Scenario: a researcher enters a project, works with a cohort, reviews history and inspection, requests an export and checks audit events.
Check permissions, true system states, data/export policies and no cross-project access.

sections.title: Pilot metrics
paragraphs: Personal: repeat check-in rate, regularity and use of practices. Organization: observation coverage, time to review a signal, percentage of events processed. Research: completion of collection waves, data quality, procedure compliance and reporting turnaround.
These are suggested KPI definitions for pilots, not achieved results claimed by Dzvin.co.

sections.title: Evidence behind a claim
paragraphs: A strong external claim needs evidence: a real working demo, an automated test, an evaluated pilot report or independent validation. If evidence is unavailable, frame the statement as a product capability or intended use.
Do not claim forecast accuracy, time savings, financial return or employee outcomes without supporting measurement.

sections.title: Demo readiness
paragraphs: Marketing needs a safe dataset with groups, records and sample events that do not contain private customer information. The PO should track exactly which screens and scenarios are stable in a test environment.
A flow that has not passed full end-to-end testing must not be labeled production-verified.

sections.title: From backlog to deck
paragraphs: Every feature slide should map to a customer problem, a specific workflow, an available screen, the intended benefit and a measurable success criterion.
Keep this chain consistent in the product specification, demonstration and external deck.

articles.title: Getting started
articles.summary: What the service does and how to begin

sections.title: Purpose
paragraphs: Dzvin.co helps people record stress, mood, energy and focus, review trends and find potentially useful wellbeing activities.
There are separate experiences for individuals, organizations and research programs.

sections.title: First steps
paragraphs: Create an account or sign in. Open My Day, complete a short self-check and review the available guidance.
Check in consistently. Trends matter more than a single daily score.

sections.title: Interpreting results
paragraphs: A single response reflects one moment, not your overall health.
Some functionality is limited by role or release stage.

sections.title: Daily checks
paragraphs: The standard check-in covers stress, mood, energy and focus on a 1–5 scale.
Notes and repeated observations offer context, but cannot establish causation.

sections.title: Suggestions and exercises
paragraphs: Relevant exercises and suggestions may follow a check-in. Personal features also support viewing history and goals.
Compare periods rather than trying to optimize one number.

sections.title: Questionnaires
paragraphs: Short psychological questionnaires may help with self-reflection.
They do not establish a diagnosis or prescribe treatment.

sections.title: Organizational use
paragraphs: The team experience helps analyze group-level changes in stress, energy and wellbeing.
Available reports and access depend on user permissions and organization settings.

sections.title: Acting on signals
paragraphs: A risk signal should prompt further contextual review, not an automated judgement about an employee.
Do not make personnel decisions from one aggregate metric. Small groups may still permit re-identification.

sections.title: Responsibilities
paragraphs: Organizations remain responsible for appropriate legal grounds for processing and transparent staff communication.
Aggregation alone does not ensure anonymity.

articles.title: Research and validation
articles.summary: Cohorts, repeated observations and evidence quality

sections.title: Research workflows
paragraphs: Research scenarios include cohort comparisons, repeated measurements and program outcome reviews.
Access to a feature does not imply independent clinical validation of every model.

sections.title: Evidence quality
paragraphs: Specify samples, metrics, windows, missing-data handling and quality criteria before analysis.
Separate correlation, prediction and causal effects. Report uncertainty.

sections.title: Access
paragraphs: Research partnerships, data scope and publishing terms are agreed separately.
Ethics and privacy requirements remain applicable.

articles.title: Privacy and data
articles.summary: Data processing, access and user rights

sections.title: Your data
paragraphs: The service may process account information, voluntary assessments and product interactions.
The current Privacy Policy defines the precise categories, purposes and legal basis.

sections.title: Workplace access
paragraphs: Organizational reports must respect permissions and applicable privacy rules.
Avoid entering unnecessary sensitive details and never share account credentials.

sections.title: Your rights
paragraphs: Use official Dzvin.co contacts to request access, correction or deletion of personal data.
This guide does not replace the Privacy Policy or Terms of Service.

articles.title: Capabilities and limitations
articles.summary: What indicators and predictions can and cannot establish

sections.title: Uncertainty
paragraphs: Self-reports may be incomplete, biased or context-dependent. Forecasts and risk indicators do not guarantee outcomes.
Recommendations are not proof of causal effects.

sections.title: Medical boundary
paragraphs: Dzvin.co is not an emergency service. It does not diagnose conditions or replace medical or psychological care.
For an immediate safety or health emergency, contact local emergency services.

sections.title: Availability
paragraphs: Some reports and modules may be role-restricted or not generally available while the product evolves.
For current availability, consult the FAQ or support team.

featuredNote: For a customer deck, start with the product story, select the buyer's segment, show a relevant demo and close with measurable success criteria.
